subject: Vocabulary
description: Homographs — same spelling, different meanings (often different pronunciations); high-frequency in CGL/IBPS reading comprehension and cloze tests.

questions.stem: Choose the meaning of 'BASS' in the sentence: 'He plays the BASS in our jazz band.'

options.option_text: A low-pitched musical instrument
A type of freshwater fish.
A leather strap or band.
A type of singing voice.

questions.explanation: BASS is a HOMOGRAPH with two distinct pronunciations and meanings: (1) /beɪs/ — a low-pitched instrument or voice (correct here); (2) /bæs/ — a fish species. CONTEXT CLUE: 'jazz band' makes the musical sense unambiguous. ETYMOLOGY: musical 'bass' from Italian 'basso' (low); fish 'bass' from Old English 'bærs'. PYQ FREQUENCY: SSC CGL Tier 2 sentence-completion uses bass/lead/object/desert as homographs ~3× per year. RELATED HOMOGRAPHS WITH PITCH-CHANGE: lead (metal /lɛd/ vs guide /liːd/); tear (rip /tɛr/ vs cry-drop /tɪr/); wind (breeze /wɪnd/ vs coil /waɪnd/); bow (arrow /boʊ/ vs bend /baʊ/). EXAMINER MINDSET: tests CONTEXTUAL READING ability — a real-world skill in legal/scientific texts where homograph misreading causes errors. INSIGHT: most English homographs descend from Old English roots that lost distinguishing accents over time, leaving spelling identical but pronunciation/meaning split.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Choose the meaning of 'OBJECT' in: 'I OBJECT to that decision strongly.'

options.option_text: To express disagreement or protest
A physical thing or item.
A goal or purpose alone alone
A grammatical noun-role alone.

questions.explanation: OBJECT is a STRESS-SHIFT HOMOGRAPH: noun /ˈɒb-dʒɛkt/ (a thing) vs verb /əb-ˈdʒɛkt/ (to oppose). The stress-pattern flips: NOUN stresses 1st syllable; VERB stresses 2nd. Same spelling, different POS, different meaning. PATTERN: many English nouns/verbs share spelling but flip stress: REcord (n) → reCORD (v); PREsent (n) → preSENT (v); SUSpect (n) → susPECT (v); CONtract (n) → conTRACT (v); INcrease (n) → inCREASE (v); REbel, REfund, EXport, IMport — all follow this rule. MEMORY TRICK: 'NOuns get NOrth-stress' (front), 'VErbs go to the VEry-end' (back). USE: 'I OBJECT to your OBJECTION' — same word, both as verb (to-OBject) and noun (the OBject of contention). EXAMINER MINDSET: tests POS recognition + stress-pattern awareness — a real skill in oral English, dictation, and listening comprehension exams (TOEFL, IELTS, Bank PO interview).
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: What does 'LEAD' mean in: 'The roof was lined with LEAD to prevent radiation leakage.'

options.option_text: A heavy metallic chemical element
To guide or direct alone alone
A small electrical wire alone alone
The first or main role alone alone

questions.explanation: LEAD has two pronunciations: /lɛd/ (the metal, atomic number 82) and /liːd/ (to guide). Context — 'roof', 'radiation' — points to the METAL. CHEMISTRY: lead has atomic number 82, density 11.34 g/cm³, melting point 327°C. Used historically for plumbing, paint, gasoline (banned now), bullets, and radiation shielding. SCIENCE LINK: lead's high density makes it excellent for blocking gamma rays and X-rays — used in hospital X-ray room walls and nuclear reactor shielding. HEALTH HAZARD: lead is a neurotoxin; childhood lead exposure causes IQ decline, irreversible. India banned leaded petrol in 2000, leaded paint phased out 2014-2016. PYQ ANGLE: 'lead vs led' (past-tense verb), 'lead' as metal vs verb — high-hit confusion in SSC error-spotting. WRITING TIP: past tense of 'lead' (verb) is 'led' — never spelled 'lead' in past tense.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: What does 'TEAR' mean in: 'Don't TEAR that important document.'

options.option_text: To rip or pull apart forcibly
A drop of liquid from eye.
To cry or weep aloud.
A momentary spree of fun.

questions.explanation: TEAR has two pronunciations: /tɛər/ (to rip — verb) and /tɪər/ (eye-water — noun). Context 'document' fixes it as the RIP verb. ETYMOLOGY DIVERGENCE: rip-tear from Old English 'teran' (to pluck/pull); eye-tear from OE 'tear'/'tæhher' (drop). Different roots, same modern spelling — coincidental homography. RELATED PAIRS: 'wound' /wuːnd/ (injury) vs 'wound' /waʊnd/ (past of wind); 'minute' /ˈmɪnɪt/ (60 sec) vs 'minute' /maɪˈnjuːt/ (very small). PYQ ANGLE: SSC CHSL frequently uses tear/wound/wind in cloze passages with disambiguating context. WRITING APPLICATION: legal documents avoid homographs deliberately; contracts use 'rip' or 'destroy' instead of 'tear' to prevent ambiguity. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests whether you can rapidly disambiguate based on surrounding noun/verb cues — a key skim-reading skill.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Choose the meaning of 'BOW' in: 'The orchestra musicians took a BOW after the performance.'

options.option_text: To bend forward in respect
A weapon for shooting arrows.
A decorative knot or ribbon.
The front of a ship alone.

questions.explanation: BOW has TWO pronunciations: /baʊ/ (to bend — verb; or front of ship — noun) and /boʊ/ (archery weapon; ribbon; violin-bow). 'Took a bow' = the BENDING gesture, /baʊ/. CULTURAL ANGLE: bowing is a universal gesture of respect — Japanese culture has elaborate hierarchy of bow depths (15° casual, 30° respectful, 45° deepest apology); Indian 'pranam' is a bow with folded hands. RELATED HOMOGRAPH: 'sow' /soʊ/ (to plant seeds) vs 'sow' /saʊ/ (female pig). VIOLIN INSIGHT: a violin bow uses horsehair (~150-200 strands per bow); rosin grips the strings. ETYMOLOGY DIVERGENCE: bend-bow from OE 'bugan'; weapon-bow from OE 'boga' — distinct roots collapsed in modern spelling. PYQ ANGLE: bow/sow/wind appear in SSC CGL Tier 2 RC passages 1-2× per session — context-clue exercises.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: What does 'WIND' mean in: 'WIND the watch carefully each night.'

options.option_text: To turn a key or coil tightly
Movement of air in atmosphere.
Breath or air in the lungs.
A sense of intuition or hint.

questions.explanation: WIND has two pronunciations: /wɪnd/ (moving air; noun) and /waɪnd/ (to coil/turn; verb). Context 'the watch' fixes it as the COILING verb /waɪnd/. MECHANICAL WATCHES: traditional pre-quartz watches had a mainspring that you'd 'wind' (coil) using the crown — typically once a day; one full wind storing ~36-48 hours of energy. AUTOMATIC WATCHES (1923 Harwood, popularized by Rolex 1931) self-wind via wrist motion + an internal rotor. SCIENCE: wind-up energy is potential elastic energy stored in a coiled metal spring (Hooke's law). RELATED COIL HOMOGRAPHS: 'wound' (past tense /waʊnd/) vs 'wound' (injury /wuːnd/); 'bind' /baɪnd/. ETYMOLOGY: 'wind' (move air) from Proto-Indo-European 'wē-' (to blow); 'wind' (coil) from PIE 'wendh-' (to turn) — separate roots. EXAM ANGLE: SSC RC passages on traditional crafts (clockmaking, weaving) frequently use 'wind' in coiling sense.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Choose the meaning of 'DESERT' in: 'Soldiers who DESERT during war face severe penalties.'

options.option_text: To abandon a duty or post
A vast dry sandy region alone
A sweet course after meals.
A reward for good deeds.

questions.explanation: DESERT has stress-shift homography: NOUN /ˈdɛzərt/ = arid land (Sahara, Thar); VERB /dɪˈzɜːrt/ = to abandon. Context 'soldiers... war' fixes it as the VERB. TRIPLE HOMOPHONE EXTENSION: 'dessert' /dɪˈzɜːrt/ (sweet course) is a HOMOPHONE of the verb 'desert' but spelled differently — distinct from 'desert' the noun (arid land). MEMORY TRICK: 'dessert has TWO Ss because you want SECONDS!' MILITARY HISTORY: desertion is a serious offense globally — under the Indian Army Act, peacetime desertion is punishable up to 7 years' imprisonment; wartime desertion can be capital. INDIAN CONSTITUTION: Art 33 allows Parliament to restrict fundamental rights of armed forces personnel — including the duty not to desert. PYQ ANGLE: desert/dessert pair appears 1× per IBPS Clerk Mains paper on average. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests stress-pattern recognition + spelling discipline.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: What does 'CLOSE' mean in the sentence: 'Please CLOSE the window; the rain is coming in'?

options.option_text: positioned very near to something or someone
to shut or seal something firmly in place
the concluding part or end of a ceremony
a narrow alleyway beside a large building

questions.explanation: In the sentence, 'CLOSE' is an imperative verb commanding someone to shut the window — Option B. Option A (positioned very near) is the adjective meaning of 'close' and is the most tempting distractor because it shares the same spelling; however, the imperative sentence structure demands a verb, not an adjective.

questions.stem: What does 'MINUTE' mean in the sentence: 'The forensic team detected MINUTE traces of poison in the victim's glass'?

options.option_text: lasting exactly sixty seconds in duration
the formal written record of a meeting
too small to be easily detected by the eye
one-sixtieth of an angular degree in measure

questions.explanation: Here 'MINUTE' is pronounced my-NYOOT and means extremely tiny or barely perceptible — Option C. Option A (sixty seconds) is the overwhelmingly familiar noun usage pronounced MIN-it, making it the prime trap; the forensic context ('traces of') signals the adjective sense, not a time unit.

questions.stem: What does 'POLISH' mean in the sentence: 'Years of stage training gave the actor a POLISH that impressed even veteran directors'?

options.option_text: relating to the people or culture of Poland
refined elegance and cultural sophistication
a substance rubbed on surfaces to make them shine
to rub a surface repeatedly until it gleams bright

questions.explanation: Here 'POLISH' is a noun meaning cultivated refinement of manner — Option B. Options C and D (the shining substance and the verb) are powerful distractors because they share the same lowercase spelling and are the more common meanings. Option A (relating to Poland) is a capitalised adjective and contextually irrelevant.

questions.stem: What does 'WOUND' mean in the sentence: 'The craftsman WOUND the copper wire tightly around the insulating core'?

options.option_text: a physical injury sustained from a cut or blow
caused deep emotional pain or hurt to someone
coiled or wrapped something tightly around a form
treated an injury by covering it with a bandage

questions.explanation: 'WOUND' here is the past tense of 'wind' (to coil), pronounced WOWND — Option C. The vast majority of test-takers read it as the noun meaning an injury (Option A, pronounced WOOND), which is the dominant everyday usage. Recognising the past-tense-of-wind reading in a manufacturing context is a classic homograph challenge.

questions.stem: What does 'CONTENT' mean in the sentence: 'She appeared CONTENT to let others take credit while she worked quietly in the background'?

options.option_text: the subject matter or information within a text
satisfied and at peace with one's situation
to fully satisfy or appease someone's desires
the proportion of a substance within a mixture

questions.explanation: 'CONTENT' functions as a predicate adjective (CON-tent) meaning satisfied or at ease — Option B. Option C (the verb 'to content') is the sharpest distractor because the verb and adjective are identically spelled; however, 'appeared CONTENT' requires an adjective complement, not a verb. Options A and D are the common noun forms used in different contexts.

questions.stem: What does 'INTIMATE' mean in the sentence: 'The spokesperson chose to INTIMATE the government's revised stance through background briefings rather than a press conference'?

options.option_text: closely acquainted in a warm and personal manner
to hint at or communicate something indirectly
having a private, cosy, or informal character
deeply personal and closely held by one person

questions.explanation: When used as a verb (in-TI-mate), 'INTIMATE' means to suggest or convey obliquely — Option B. Almost all candidates know 'intimate' only as the adjective meaning close or personal (Options A, C, D), making this a severe homograph trap. The verb form appears in formal diplomatic and administrative language — precisely the register favoured by SSC CGL and IBPS PO paper-setters.

questions.stem: What does 'INCENSE' mean in the sentence: 'The sudden cancellation of earned leave managed to INCENSE the entire workforce at the plant'?

options.option_text: a fragrant resin or stick burned to release aroma
to fill a place with smoke of a ritual substance
to make someone extremely angry or deeply enraged
a ceremonial offering used in religious worship rites

questions.explanation: As a verb (in-SENS), 'INCENSE' means to provoke intense anger — Option C. The noun 'IN-cense' (fragrant substance burned in worship) is what nearly all candidates recall first, making Options A and D powerful distractors. Recognising that the identical spelling functions as a verb meaning to enrage requires the precise homograph awareness tested at CGL Tier-II and IBPS PO Mains level.
